segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a series dedicated to one of the greatest, strangest, most magnificent novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be reading Bleak House closely — its fog, its law, its secrets, its people — with three remarkable guides.

First: Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, lifelong defender of Dickens' moral imagination, and a man who will politely demolish any reading he considers reductive — including, quite possibly, several of mine.

Second: Professor James Blackstone, legal historian, whose knowledge of Victorian institutions — what Chancery actually was, what poverty actually meant — will keep us honest whenever the novel threatens to become merely literary.

And third: Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any person living — who approaches every page of Bleak House as a performer first and a critic a very close second.
Today we begin at the beginning — with the fog.
Dickens opens Bleak House not with a character, not with a scene, but with a condition — a fog so total that it seems to swallow the whole of England, and London in particular.
Edmund, let's begin with you — what do you make of that famous opening, and what is Dickens actually doing there?
What Dickens is doing, I think, is something rather more precise than is generally acknowledged.
The fog is not, as some eager critics would have it, a metaphor for capitalism, or for the obfuscations of power.
It is, first and foremost, a literary device — and a supremely confident one.
Dickens is establishing a moral atmosphere — one in which clarity itself is the rarest and most precious quality.
And into that atmosphere he will place individuals — Esther, Jarndyce, Richard — whose moral visibility, or invisibility, is the real subject of the novel.
Dr. Johnson observed that the greatness of a work lies not in its subject but in what the author makes of it.
Dickens makes of his fog a world — and that is the measure of his genius.
James, you've spent a career studying the institutions Dickens is writing about — and I wonder whether, from your vantage point, the fog feels like something more literal than Edmund allows.
Edmund is right that it is a literary device — I wouldn't dispute that for a moment.
But the fog is also — and I think Dickens knew this perfectly well — a documentary fact.
London in the eighteen-fifties produced a particular kind of coal-smoke fog — a 'pea-souper,' as they were called — that genuinely blinded the city for days at a time.
And Chancery — the real Court of Chancery — was itself a kind of institutional fog.
Cases ran for decades — sometimes longer than the lifetimes of the original litigants — consuming estates entirely in legal fees.
The Jarndyce and Jarndyce case is not a satirical exaggeration — it is barely a composite.
When Dickens writes that 'this scarecrow of a suit has, in course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means,' he is reporting, not inventing.
'the scarecrow of a suit... has, in course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means.'
That is not hyperbole — that is a precise description of how the system worked.
I love that both of you are correct — and I'd add that from where I stand, as a performer, the fog is also simply magnificent to read aloud.
The rhythm of that opening page — 'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river... fog down the river' — it's incantatory.
'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
Dickens wrote for the voice — I am absolutely convinced of it — and that passage proves it on every syllable.
But there's something else in the novel about fog and disguise that I think is worth our attention — and it's rather darker.
Dickens returns to the idea of concealment — of things hidden not by weather but by respectability — and it becomes genuinely sinister.
There's a passage describing the criminal colony around Leicester Square — and the writing is extraordinary.
'he is a more designing, callous, and intolerable devil when he sticks a pin in his shirt-front, calls himself a gentleman, backs a card or colour, plays a game or so of billiards.'
The devil in fustian — that's one thing. The devil in a gentleman's shirt-front — that, Dickens says, is something altogether worse.
Oliver puts his finger on something I would not wish to dismiss — and I concede it freely.
Dickens is not naïve about class — he never was.
But I would argue that what concerns him is not class as a system — it is the moral corruption that respectability can license.
Consider Tulkinghorn — the novel's great cold villain — described by the narrator with a beautiful, withering irony.
'The peerage may have warmer worshippers and faithfuller believers than Mr. Tulkinghorn, after all, if everything were known.'
That phrase — 'if everything were known' — is the moral crux of the entire novel.
Bleak House is a novel about concealment — and what is concealed is always, in the end, a question of character.
Edmund's reading of Tulkinghorn is compelling — though I'd note that Tulkinghorn's power derives entirely from his institutional position.
He knows what he knows because the law gives him access — to houses, to correspondence, to private lives.
His personal moral character and his professional function are inseparable — which is precisely Dickens' point.
The system does not merely attract Tulkinghorns — it produces them.
And James, that is exactly what makes him so terrifying to read aloud.
There's no theatrical menace to Tulkinghorn — no villain's flourish — just that extraordinary description: 'In manner, close and dry. In voice, husky and low. In face, watchful behind a blind.'
'In manner, close and dry. In voice, husky and low. In face, watchful behind a blind.'
Three short clauses — barely a sentence — and you have one of the most frightening men in English fiction.
That is what I mean when I say Dickens wrote for the voice — the syntax itself is the characterisation.
Fog, concealment, respectability as disguise — and behind it all, the grinding machinery of the law.
Coming up, we'll turn to the characters who must navigate that machinery — and what it costs them.

segments.title: Richard's Slow Dissolution: A Gentleman Unmade

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, where we take Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart, chapter by chapter, theme by theme.
I'm your host, and today we're examining one of the novel's most quietly devastating storylines: the slow ruin of Richard Carstone.
A young man of genuine promise, destroyed not by villainy but by a lawsuit, and by something darker in his own character.
With me today are three extraordinary guides to Bleak House.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, lifelong admirer of Dickens' moral imagination, and a man who reads Richard Carstone as a study in the weakness of will.
Professor James Blackstone — legal historian, expert on Victorian institutions, who will remind us what Chancery actually was and what it did to real people.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive, who hears in Richard's story the cadences Dickens wrote for the speaking voice.
To understand what Chancery does to Richard Carstone, we need to understand what Richard was before it took hold.
Oliver, you've spent more time inside Dickens' prose than almost any living person — where does Richard's story begin?
It begins, I think, in the warmth of Bleak House itself — that extraordinary opening where Jarndyce introduces the young people to their world and their prospects.
And the passage I keep returning to isn't even about Richard directly — it's Jarndyce describing Boythorn, of all people.
But listen to how he addresses Richard — 'Rick' — alongside Ada and 'little Cobweb,' meaning Esther.
"Rick—and Ada, and little Cobweb too, for you are all interested in a visitor."
That's Jarndyce at his most paternal — all three of them are folded into a kind of provisional family.
And Richard, in this moment, is simply 'Rick' — not yet Richard the heir, not yet Richard the claimant.
There's such tenderness in that nickname, and Dickens knows exactly what he's doing — he's showing us what will be lost.
Oliver puts his finger on something essential, and I'd press it a little further.
The nickname 'Rick' is not merely affectionate — it is diagnostic.
Richard has not yet been required to become Richard.
Dickens is extraordinarily attentive to the moral weight of character formation — the question of what a young man does with his freedom.
Burke would have recognised it: the education of the gentleman requires friction, adversity, resistance.
What Richard receives instead is a lawsuit — and a lawsuit, as Dickens understood, is the antithesis of moral education.
It substitutes perpetual expectation for effort, drift for decision, a horizon that forever recedes.
Edmund is quite right about the lawsuit as moral trap, and I want to supply the institutional scaffolding beneath it.
Because Dickens wasn't inventing a metaphor — Jarndyce and Jarndyce is a composite portrait of real cases that ran for generations.
And there's a moment very early in the novel where Dickens, through old Krook, gives us the most economical diagnosis of what Chancery actually does to human beings.
Tom Jarndyce — the man who shot himself — put it this way:
"It's being ground to bits in a slow mill; it's being roasted at a slow fire; it's being stung to death by single bees; it's being drowned by drops; it's going mad by grains."
That accumulation — mill, fire, bees, drops, grains — is not rhetoric for its own sake.
It precisely captures the phenomenology of attrition — how institutional delay kills not with a blow but with a thousand postponements.
And that is the mechanism working on Richard Carstone throughout the novel.
'Going mad by grains' — I've read that passage hundreds of times and it still catches me unprepared.
What Dickens understands as a prose artist is that rhythm enacts meaning — those five parallel clauses build exactly the sensation they describe.
By the fifth repetition you feel the grind yourself.
And Richard's dissolution follows precisely that pattern — no single catastrophe, just the slow diminishment of a man by instalments.
Now, Skimpole is the interesting foil here — a man who has simply exempted himself from all that grinding.
Esther watches him and is bewildered, but she puts it perfectly:
"I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them. That he WAS free of them, I scarcely doubted; he was so very clear about it himself."
Skimpole has found a way to live in perpetual expectation without suffering its corrosive effects — because he simply doesn't acknowledge debts, to people or to life.
Richard can't manage that trick — he still has enough of a conscience to be destroyed by what he's waiting for.
The Skimpole comparison is very illuminating, and I think it reveals exactly why I resist the purely institutional reading of Richard's fall.
Skimpole and Richard are both caught in the Chancery orbit — but Skimpole is not destroyed, and Richard is.
The difference is not the institution — the difference is character.
Richard has the capacity for genuine attachment — to Ada, to Esther, to Jarndyce — and that very capacity makes him vulnerable in a way Skimpole, the perfect egotist, simply is not.
Dr. Johnson observed that the chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too strong to be broken.
Richard's habit is hope — corrupted, delusional hope — and by the time he perceives its weight, it has already done its work.
I take Edmund's point, and I don't want to flatten the question of character — Richard is not simply a victim.
But I want to insist that the system is designed to consume people like Richard — and that Dickens knew it, and said so with surgical precision.
There's a passage involving Mr. Vholes and Mr. Kenge that is, in my view, among the most devastatingly accurate pieces of institutional satire in the English language.
Kenge is explaining why reform of Chancery is simply impossible:

"Alter this law, sir, and what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes?
Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
'Swept from the face of the earth' — said with such magnificent moral alarm, as though the extinction of Vholes were a catastrophe to rival the Flood.
And then — and this is the masterstroke — the parliamentary committee inquiry collapses entirely when one witness confirms that Vholes is 'a most respectable man.'
Respectability is the system's immune response — it rejects every reform before it can take hold.
And Richard, by engaging Vholes, does not just employ a solicitor — he plugs himself into that machine.
'A most respectable man' — and the inquiry dies for ten years.
Dickens is doing something technically remarkable there — he's written a mock parliamentary transcript that reads funnier and more savagely than any actual Hansard.
And Vholes himself — good Lord, Vholes — is one of the great quiet monsters of Victorian fiction.
He never raises his voice, he never makes a promise he can't keep — he simply attends to Richard's ruin with perfect professional diligence.
The comedy and the horror are entirely intertwined — which is where Dickens is, at his very best, absolutely incomparable.
I should like to turn, if I may, to a passage that illuminates what is at stake in Richard's dissolution from a rather different angle — the portrait of Bucket attending Sir Leicester.
Dickens gives us Bucket as a whist player holding a winning hand — and the comparison rewards close attention.

"From the expression of his face he might be a famous whist-player for a large stake — say a hundred guineas certain — with the game in his hand, but with a high reputation involved in his playing his hand out to the last card in a masterly way."
Bucket has mastery — over his face, his knowledge, his moment.
Richard has its precise opposite — a man who holds cards he cannot read, in a game whose rules keep changing.
The one exercises will; the other is subject to it.
That contrast between Bucket and Richard is one Dickens sets up with great deliberateness, and I think it cuts both ways.
Bucket is a professional — a man whose instincts have been honed by a particular institution, the detective branch of the Metropolitan Police, itself newly formed in the 1840s.
Chancery produces no such formation — it produces only drift and attrition.
The detective and the claimant are the novel's two faces of institutional life — one is made by his institution, the other consumed by his.
There's something almost unbearable in that symmetry — Bucket, sharpened to an instrument of purpose, and Richard, ground to nothing by the same legal world.
Edmund, James, Oliver — thank you.
We'll return in the next segment to ask what Richard's story tells us about Dickens' vision of gentlemanly virtue — and whether he saw any way out.

segments.title: The Weight of Secrets: Lady Dedlock's Reckoning

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart sentence by sentence — and puts it back together again.
Today we're inside the world of secrets — the slow, terrible pressure that Lady Dedlock lives under, and the machinery of class and law that makes her predicament possible.
With me, as ever, are three guides I trust absolutely.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, Dickens's moral defender, the man who will remind us that character, not circumstance, is the true subject of this novel.
Professor James Blackstone — legal historian, who knows what Chancery actually was, what it did to real lives, and why Dickens was not exaggerating.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any living person, who hears the rhythms of this prose the way a musician hears a score.
We begin, I think, with Sir Leicester — that magnificent, absurd, and ultimately rather moving figure at the centre of the Dedlock world.
Edmund, you've always argued that Dickens treats Sir Leicester with more genuine respect than he's usually given credit for. Where do you begin?
The critical temptation, always, is to read Sir Leicester as pure satire — Dickens skewering the aristocracy.
And there is satire — magnificent satire, I grant you entirely.
Dickens tells us, with that perfect deadpan, that Sir Leicester has a general opinion that the world might get on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks.
The self-importance is comic, yes — but Dickens does not leave it there.
He gives us, in the same breath, a man of strict conscience, disdainful of all littleness and meanness.
That final formulation — honourable, obstinate, truthful, high-spirited, intensely prejudiced, perfectly unreasonable — is not mockery alone.
It is Dickens acknowledging that the human being contains contradictions — and that the contradictions themselves command a kind of regard.
What I love — and Edmund is absolutely right about this — is the rhythm of that list.
Honourable, obstinate, truthful, high-spirited — you think you know where it's going, you're almost nodding along approvingly.
And then — intensely prejudiced, perfectly unreasonable — bang, bang.
Two quiet bombs, placed with absolute surgical precision.
That is Dickens writing for the voice, not the page — he knows an actor needs those two beats at the end.
And it's also, in performance, unexpectedly tender — you find yourself almost fond of him by the time you reach 'unreasonable.'
The tenderness is real — and historically it matters.
Dickens is not writing a polemic against the aristocracy as a class — he is writing about what happens to individuals who are formed entirely by an institution.
Sir Leicester was not a bad man — by his own lights, he was a very good one.
The catastrophe is that his lights were set so narrow — by birth, by rank, by the whole architecture of Chesney Wold.
And Chesney Wold itself becomes the argument — that extraordinary passage about the oaks and the ivy.
Dickens gives us Sir Leicester's world not merely described but felt — you sense the weight of those centuries.
One does not mock that language — one inhabits it.
Dickens understood that a world which produces that beauty is not simply wrong — it is tragically, fatally limited.
'Umbrageous oaks' — I ask you.
Most writers would have written 'shady' and moved on.
Dickens chooses 'umbrageous' — and suddenly the whole sentence smells of old leaves.
That's the verbal sensuousness Edmund is pointing to — Dickens's prose doing the work of architecture.
But then — and this is the thing — you come out of that beautiful fog and find Sir Leicester sitting in his easy chair, opposing his repose to the restless flights of ironmasters.
And 'opposing his repose' — it's magnificent and it's pitiful at exactly the same moment.
Let's turn, then, to the room where the real drama of secrets is conducted — Lady Dedlock's own drawing room, with Tulkinghorn always in the corner.
Edmund — there's a passage in chapter twenty-nine that I find quietly devastating: Sir Leicester reading aloud to his wife, apparently the picture of domestic contentment.
Yes — and it is devastating precisely because of what Dickens withholds.
Sir Leicester sits in my Lady's room — that room in which Tulkinghorn had already read the document that began to unravel everything.
He is, the narrator tells us, particularly complacent — and she sits before the fire with her screen in her hand, as she had sat that other day.
And Sir Leicester reads from his newspaper — a man with a well-balanced mind, he says of the author, nodding at the fire as if nodding down at the man from a mount.
That 'from a mount' — it is everything, isn't it.
He is not in his drawing room — in his own imagination, he is always on elevated ground.
Meanwhile Lady Dedlock sits, screen in hand, holding herself entirely still — the image of a woman who has learned to make her face a second screen.
That image of the screen is one of the novel's great recurring objects.
Historically, a fire-screen in a Victorian interior was a practical thing — you shielded your complexion from the heat.
Dickens makes it a psychological instrument — she holds it to shield not her complexion but her expression.
And the room itself carries history — Dickens tells us, almost parenthetically, that this is the same room where Tulkinghorn read the fateful affidavit.
It is Dickens doing what only the greatest novelists do — using the same furniture, the same chairs, the same fireplace, to accumulate moral weight.
And it's the same room in which Tulkinghorn will later deliver the extraordinary portrait scene — chapter thirty-nine.
That scene — I have read it aloud perhaps two dozen times and it still makes me want to put the book down and simply stare.
Tulkinghorn stands with his back to the chimney-piece, lifts his glasses — and turns, apparently at random, to Lady Dedlock's portrait.
"Who is this? 'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character."
Good day to you, gentlemen. Good day.
And he leaves.
He doesn't accuse her. He doesn't threaten her. He simply pronounces judgement on her portrait — and walks out.
'Wants force of character' — one must sit with that phrase for a moment.
In Tulkinghorn's mouth, it is a lawyer's verdict — precise, almost clinical.
But what it also does — with that opening 'Ha!' — is mimic the cadence of connoisseurship, of a man passing through a gallery and pronouncing with indifferent authority.
He is not talking about the portrait at all, of course.
He is talking about Lady Dedlock herself — and she knows it, and he knows she knows it — and yet nothing has been said.
That is the Tulkinghorn method — the exercise of power by implication, never by declaration.
And that method is not merely a character trait — it is a professional technique.
Victorian lawyers — particularly solicitors acting for great families — held their power through the accumulation of secrets.
The Tulkinghorn relationship to the Dedlocks is not unusual for the period — he is the family lawyer, he knows everything, and that knowledge is his power.
What Dickens does — brilliantly — is dramatise what that relationship actually feels like for the person on the other side of it.
Lady Dedlock cannot dismiss him, cannot expose him, cannot buy him off — he is too embedded in the structure of her life.
And there's another kind of institutional weight pressing down in this novel — the Chancery itself, which Dickens makes almost a twin to the Dedlock world.
James — you've spent your career studying that court. How does Dickens' version hold up?
Remarkably well — which is a sobering thing to have to say.
The Court of Chancery in the eighteen-forties and fifties was genuinely a machine for consuming lives — suits in Chancery lasted generations, costs devoured estates.
Mr. Kenge's phrase — 'a monument of Chancery practice' — is Dickens catching a real register of professional self-satisfaction.
Lawyers genuinely spoke this way — the complexity of a case was a source of pride, not shame.
But the most extraordinary figure for the Chancery — the one I return to again and again — is Krook.
Krook, surrounded by his parchments and his rust and his must, who tells Esther with perfect straightforwardness —
That four-word sentence contains the whole critique — and it arrives from the mouth of a man surrounded by everything the law has produced and abandoned.
'We both grub on in a muddle' — I've been saying that sentence to myself for thirty years.
What's extraordinary about Krook as a character is the sheer delight he takes in being what he is.
He doesn't know he can't read — or rather, he doesn't feel it as lack.
He has his parchments, he has his cat Lady Jane — magnificent name, Lady Jane, for that particular cat — and he has his lantern.
And he goes to observe his 'noble and learned brother' in the court — the Lord Chancellor himself — without the faintest trace of irony.
The parallel is not Dickens nudging you — it is the whole world of the novel manifesting in one glorious grotesque.
Oliver is right to resist calling it a nudge — it is not a nudge, it is a structural rhyme.
The whole architecture of Bleak House proceeds by these rhymes — high and low reflecting each other, the great house and the rag-and-bottle shop, Tulkinghorn and Krook.
What is perhaps undervalued is how morally serious those rhymes are.
Dickens is not saying 'the aristocracy is exactly like a junk shop' — he is saying that the same human tendencies — hoarding, paralysis, the refusal to let go — manifest at every level of society.
'All's fish that comes to my net' — Krook says it of his own shop, but it is equally true of Chancery, and of Tulkinghorn himself.
And with that image — the net drawing everything in and letting nothing go — I think we've found the heart of what this segment has been circling.

Lady Dedlock trapped in her drawing room, Sir Leicester reading from his paper on a mount, Tulkinghorn passing judgement on a portrait, Krook in his shop grubbing alongside his noble and learned brother.
Different rooms, different classes — the same muddle.
In our next segment, we'll follow the secrets further — out of the great house entirely, into the fog and the streets, and to the figure Dickens places at the very bottom of this world.
Do stay with us.

segments.title: The Street Arab and the System: Jo's Testimony

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens' great novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with genuine pleasure.

I'm your host, and today we're looking at some of the novel's most morally charged material — Jo the crossing-sweeper, Gridley the man from Shropshire, and the slippery, beaming figure of Harold Skimpole.
Three figures who illuminate, each in their own way, what the system does to people — and what some people do to avoid noticing.
With me today are three exceptional guides to this territory.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes that Dickens' true subject is always individual character — what people are made of, when it counts.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — he knows what Chancery actually was, what it cost, and who paid that cost.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than almost anyone alive — he reads this novel as a performer, and hears things the rest of us miss.
Let's begin with Jo — specifically with a passage near the end of his life, in George's shooting gallery, surrounded by the unlikely constellation of people his brief existence has drawn together.
Oliver, you know this passage well. What do you hear in it?
What I hear, first of all, is Dickens the great marshaller of souls — assembling this cast around a dying boy with the instincts of a stage manager.
Phil Squod, Jarndyce, Woodcourt, Trooper George — each one enormous in their own right, each one diminished to witness by what's happening to Jo.
But what strikes me every time I read it aloud is the sentence at the centre — let me find it.
"Both thinking, much, how strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast in the web of very different lives."
That word — entangled. Dickens doesn't say 'connected.' He doesn't say 'touched.'
He says entangled — which implies struggle, constraint, something that cannot be easily undone.
And then look at Phil Squod — smoky gunpowder visage, one eyebrow, the little green-baize cap — all of that comic grotesque energy, and then he says: 'Hold up, my boy. Hold up.'
Four words. And the whole novel is in them.
Oliver is quite right about the word 'entangled,' and I'd go further.
The web is not merely fate's mechanism — it is Dickens' argument about moral responsibility.
Each person in that room has been given an opportunity to respond to Jo — and Dickens judges them by how they take it.
Woodcourt passes the test magnificently. Jarndyce, as ever, passes it quietly and without display.
The Trooper — General George — is described as 'filling the doorway with his athletic figure' and shedding 'temporary vigour' upon Jo.
"From his superfluity of life and strength, seeming to shed down temporary vigour upon Jo."
'Superfluity' — that is the precise word. George has more life than he needs, and he gives the surplus to the boy.
This is Dickens' morality at its most luminous — not a system, not a programme, but individual human generosity meeting individual human need.
I don't wish to dampen Edmund's warmth towards individual virtue — it is entirely warranted in that room.

But I want to note something about that assembly: it consists entirely of people outside the institutions — the armourer, the doctor working without a fashionable practice, the guardsman turned shooting-gallery keeper.
The people who are inside the institutions — Chancery, the Commissioners, the parish — are conspicuously absent from that room.
Which is, I think, Dickens' point — not only that individuals can be good, but that institutions systematically prevent them from being so.
And this connects directly to Gridley — to the man who was ground up by those same institutions and who refused, to his cost, to pretend otherwise.
Which brings us to Gridley — and to what might be the most ferociously honest speech in the entire novel.
James, you've lived with this passage. Tell us what Gridley's defiance actually means — legally, historically.
Gridley is not a fictional exaggeration. That is the thing people always need to understand first.
Dickens based him on cases he had personally observed — men whose entire adult lives were consumed by Chancery suits they had inherited and could not escape.
The Court of Chancery, in the early Victorian period, was catastrophically backed up — suits ran for decades, costs swallowed estates entire.
And Gridley articulates something that contemporary reformers were also saying — that the system drove reasonable men to apparent unreason.
He says — and this is the passage that stops me every time — let me read it as he would have spoken it.
"If I did restrain myself I should become imbecile. I was a good-enough-tempered man once, I believe."
That 'I believe' — that small, devastating qualifier — is a man trying to remember who he was before the law took him.
And then the great vow — the one that makes Gridley unforgettable.
"I'll shame them. To the last, I'll show myself in that court to its shame."

"If I knew when I was going to die, and could be carried there, and had a voice to speak with, I would die there, saying, 'You have brought me here and sent me from here many and many a time. Now send me out feet foremost!'"
Feet foremost. That is a man who has decided that his death will be his final argument.
There is no legal remedy available to him — so he transforms his own body into a piece of testimony.
'Feet foremost' — James, when you read that, I genuinely feel the theatrical genius of it.
Dickens trained himself as a stenographer in these courts. He sat there, he watched, he took down the words.
And so Gridley's speech has that authenticity — it sounds like a man speaking in fury, not an author constructing a speech in fury.
The rhythm of it — 'I have been in prison for contempt of court. I have been in prison for threatening the solicitor' — that's not rhetoric.
That's a man counting his losses on his fingers, quietly, so he doesn't lose control before he's finished.
There is something Johnson-like about Gridley, which I find genuinely moving.
Johnson, too, knew what it was to struggle against institutions that diminished a man and to refuse, on grounds of simple self-respect, to pretend they had not.
What interests me, though, is Esther's narration of this scene. She witnesses Gridley and she does not moralize about him.
She simply records. And that restraint is itself a moral judgment — it says: this man's anger is legitimate, it does not require my gloss.
Dickens, through Esther, practices a courtesy towards Gridley that the Court of Chancery never could.
And then we have Skimpole — who is the system's most cheerful accomplice, because he has simply decided not to notice any of it.
Edmund, there's a passage where Skimpole expounds his philosophy of self-acceptance — and Sir Leicester Dedlock, quite separately, reveals that Skimpole has been sightseeing at Chesney Wold.
What does putting these two passages together tell us about how Dickens constructed this character?
Skimpole is Dickens' most devastating portrait — and I say this as someone constitutionally suspicious of Dickens when he turns polemical.
Because with Skimpole, he never argues. He simply shows.
The philosophy Skimpole announces — his famous self-acceptance — is stated with the serene confidence of a man who has never been questioned.
"What Harold Skimpole was, Harold Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he first made his own acquaintance."
'To his considerable surprise' — that detail is the whole man.
He discovered himself as one might discover an amusing stranger at a dinner party, and has been dining out on the acquaintance ever since.
And the Chesney Wold episode — Sir Leicester puzzling through Skimpole's name with his eyeglass, those magnificent stumbles — Skampling, Skumpling — and then delivering his grave complaint.
"A gentleman who would appear to possess a cultivated taste for the fine arts, was likewise deterred... from examining the family pictures with that leisure, that attention, that care."
That triple rhythm — 'that leisure, that attention, that care' — is Sir Leicester's entire worldview encapsulated: life as a ceremonial obligation owed to art, to lineage, to form.
And Skimpole, whose whole performance rests on being untethered from all such obligations, has apparently been helping himself to the pictures anyway.
I have to say — reading Skimpole aloud is one of the great guilty pleasures of the Dickens canon.
The prose itself chirps — Dickens even uses that word, 'chirped' — and you feel the danger of enjoying him too much, which is precisely the trap Esther and Jarndyce fall into.
He imagines Jo becoming Lord Mayor and establishing the Summerson Almshouses — and it is genuinely funny, and you laugh, and then you feel slightly sick.
Because Jo is dying three chapters away, and Skimpole has already sold him to Bucket for five pounds.
The comedy is Dickens' method of making the horror bearable enough that you keep reading — and then the horror lands all the harder for it.
What strikes me about Skimpole, from a structural point of view, is that he is the ideological mirror of Chancery.
Chancery consumes resources and produces nothing — it processes, it deliberates, it defers, and at the end there is nothing left to distribute.
Skimpole does exactly the same thing — he absorbs the goodwill, the money, the patience of everyone around him, and returns charm, which is non-transferable and does not pay rent.
The philosophy he enunciates — that he has 'accepted himself with all his failings' as 'sound philosophy' — is a precise description of what institutions do when they cease to reform.
They accept themselves. They make the best of the bargain. And Jo moves on.
That is a remarkable formulation — Skimpole as institutional self-acceptance made flesh.
Edmund, does that reading trouble you — or does it actually square with your sense of what Dickens was doing?
It troubles me only slightly — and I'll say why.
James is right that Skimpole rhymes with the system. I accept that entirely as a structural observation.
But Dickens is also doing something more personal and more precise — Skimpole is a portrait of Leigh Hunt, and everyone in his circle knew it.
Which means that Skimpole's evil — and it is evil, by the end — is not the evil of a system but the evil of a particular kind of egotism dressed as innocence.
Dickens is saying: the system is bad, yes. But so is the man who uses the system's badness as permission for his own.
Individual character remains the irreducible thing. The system does not excuse Skimpole. Nothing does.
And Dickens knew it, too — he was uncomfortable with the Leigh Hunt resemblance for years afterwards.
There's a letter in which he rather guiltily insists that Skimpole's vices are quite different from Hunt's virtues.
Which reads rather like Skimpole's own philosophy — I have accepted myself with all my failings and thought it sound.
Oliver — perfect. We'll leave Skimpole there, which is more than Jarndyce managed.

What has emerged from this passage is a kind of triptych — Jo, who has no philosophy and no protection; Gridley, who has fury and nothing else; and Skimpole, who has philosophy in abundance and uses it to avoid everything.
Together they map the moral terrain of Bleak House with extraordinary precision.
Thank you to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan.
We'll be back with more Bleak House Unpacked very soon.

segments.title: Bleak House at Full Tilt: Comedy, Bureaucracy, and Chaos

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — the programme that takes Dickens' most ambitious novel apart, page by page, room by room, and fog bank by fog bank.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at a quality that doesn't always get its due in discussions of Bleak House: its sheer, anarchic, gloriously managed comic energy.
The fog, the Chancery, the moral weight — all of that is present.
But so is Krook, and Smallweed, and a court full of people convinced there are guineas pouring out of tea-pots.
To unpack all of this, I'm joined by three quite extraordinary company.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has been reading Dickens with rigorous moral seriousness for longer than most of us have been alive — and who will, I suspect, defend the fog as a literary device before the hour is out.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows Chancery from the inside out — the real institution, its real victims, and its real legacy.
And Oliver Trevelyan has read more Dickens aloud than almost any person living — he hears the comic rhythms that silent readers miss, and he brings them here with us today.
Let's begin with the domestic heart of the novel — Bleak House itself, and the extraordinary passage in which Esther first takes it in.
What strikes me, every time I return to that passage, is how Dickens earns sentimentality — which is quite a different thing from simply indulging it.

Esther's description of the rooms is built on a principle of magnificent incongruity — birds staring at a real trout in a case, portraits of young brides aged into grey old women across different rooms.
It is comic, yes — but the comedy is in the service of warmth.
And then Dickens lifts it, at the close of the passage, into something close to prose poetry.
"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw"
That word — brightening — does an enormous amount of work.
It is Jarndyce's character illuminating the physical world, not the other way around.
That is the moral imagination at work — and it is, I would insist, what separates Dickens from mere satirists.
Edmund, I'm entirely with you on the brightness — but I want to linger, if I may, on those birds staring at the trout.
Because that is Dickens writing for performance, not for the page.
When you read it aloud — really commit to it — the rhythm of that list is almost musical.
A real trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with gravy.
"Served with gravy" — that is a joke, and it lands differently every single time, depending on the weight you put on it.
The comedy in this novel is never merely decorative.
It is structural — it builds the world we then inhabit when things get very dark indeed.
I want to come at it from a slightly different angle, if I may.
The description of Bleak House as warm, hospitable, irregular — it's doing something very pointed in contrast to what Jarndyce immediately describes just chapters later.
He takes Esther through the wreckage that Chancery has made of property in London.

"It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder"
Now, the historical record confirms this almost exactly.
Chancery suits could paralyse property for decades — title unresolved, no one able to sell, repair, or demolish.
The houses literally fell in on themselves while lawyers extracted fees from the estate.
Dickens is not exaggerating.
I wouldn't dispute the historical accuracy for a moment — James is quite right about that.
But notice what Dickens does with the rhetoric of that passage — it is not mere reportage, however accurate.
"Every door might be death's door."
That parenthetical aside is a moment of pure moral poetry — and it arrives almost casually, mid-catalogue.
And then Jarndyce adds: "These are the Great Seal's impressions, my dear, all over England — the children know them."
That final phrase — the children know them — is devastating precisely because it is so quiet.
It is not polemical.
It is something far worse — it is resigned.
That balance — between the comic and the devastating, between the warm interior and the crumbling street outside — runs through the whole novel.
And nowhere is that comic register more brilliant than when Dickens turns his eye to the spectacle of collective human absurdity.
Oliver — the Smallweed episode, and what the court imagines is hidden in Krook's shop.
Oh, this passage is pure joy — I mean that with complete seriousness, because Dickens is working at absolute full tilt here.
The whole court has gone mad with speculation about what Smallweed is finding in Krook's possessions.
Dickens describes it in this marvellous sweep of collective delirium.
"Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop."
A Fortunatus' purse — bottomless, self-replenishing — it's the perfect image for gossip that feeds on itself.
And then the fantasy escalates: guineas pouring out of tea-pots, crown-pieces overflowing punch-bowls, mattresses stuffed with Bank of England notes.
The rhythm builds like a music-hall routine — and then it comes to earth with: they discovered nothing.
What I find historically resonant in that passage is how accurately Dickens captures the function of gossip in close, overcrowded urban courts.
These were communities in which almost no one had money, almost everyone knew each other's business, and the fantasy of discovered wealth was genuinely intoxicating.
Dickens captures even the mechanics of how rumour becomes entertainment — Little Swills at the pub, gags in the Harmonic nights, Miss Melvilleson pointing her song towards next door.
It is a community creating meaning from nothing — which is, of course, what Chancery does too.
James — that's exactly it, and it connects to another figure I want to bring in: Tulkinghorn.
Because the comedy of the court is one kind of chaos — gregarious, collective, noisy.
Tulkinghorn is the opposite of all of that — and Dickens describes him in a way that is almost comic in its very stillness.
There's a sentence about his movements between Chesney Wold and his chambers that I find genuinely uncanny.
"He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields."
He doesn't travel — he simply appears.
There's something almost supernatural in the prose — and when you read it aloud, that quality becomes genuinely chilling.
I think Oliver has identified something important about the architecture of this novel's tonal range.
The chaos of the court, the gossip, the absurdity of Smallweed — all of that is rendered with affectionate comedy.
But Tulkinghorn operates in an entirely different register — one of cold, procedural menace.
He neither changes his dress before the journey nor talks of it afterwards — that sentence alone is a character study.
A man who leaves no trace of experience — who does not allow life to mark him — is either a saint or a monster.
Dickens leaves us in very little doubt as to which.
There's a legal dimension to Tulkinghorn's blankness that I think is worth naming.
The Victorian solicitor — particularly those managing great landed families — operated precisely through this studied impermeability.
To be trusted with secrets, you had to become, visibly and habitually, a person who did not react to them.
Dickens understood this intuitively, I think — and he made it sinister precisely by pushing it to its logical extreme.
A man who melts in and out of rooms — and a court that invents treasure where there is none.
Both, in their different ways, are images of how power — or the idea of power — circulates through this novel.
We'll return after the break to look at the novel's stranger territories — Krook's shop, spontaneous combustion, and the gothic underbelly of that comic surface.

segments.title: The Machinery of Injustice: Chancery and Class

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart, chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
I'm your host, and today we're turning to one of the novel's great subjects — the Court of Chancery, and what Dickens makes of it as a machine for grinding people down.
With me today are three people who know this novel with unusual depth and from very different angles.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and literary critic of the old school — he reads Bleak House as a great moral novel, and he tends to be suspicious of readings that turn Dickens into a pamphleteer.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who specialises in Victorian institutions — he knows what Chancery actually was, and what it meant in practice for the people caught inside it.

And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than I dare count — he comes to the prose as a performer, hearing the rhythms and the timing that the page alone can't quite capture.
James, let's begin with you — because before we can talk about what Dickens does with Chancery, perhaps we should establish what Chancery actually was.
Thank you — and it's worth being precise here, because the reality is almost as grotesque as Dickens makes it appear.
The Court of Chancery was the court of equity — the court that handled matters the common law couldn't reach: trusts, wills, inheritances, disputed estates.
In principle, it existed to deliver justice where rigid legal rules would produce manifest unfairness.

In practice, by the early nineteenth century it had become almost entirely dysfunctional — cases lasted decades, costs accumulated without limit, and the original parties frequently died before any judgment was reached.
Dickens opens the novel with a scene that captures this precisely — the wretched population that haunts the court, waiting for something that will never come.
There is a little mad old woman in a squeezed bonnet who is always in court, from its sitting to its rising, and always expecting some incomprehensible judgment to be given in her favour.
Some say she really is, or was, a party to a suit, but no one knows for certain because no one cares.
That last clause — 'no one cares' — is as cold as anything in the novel.
The system doesn't need to be actively malicious to destroy people — indifference does the work perfectly well.
And it's worth noting that Dickens isn't writing a pamphlet there — he's writing a gallery of portraits, each one slightly more desolate than the last.

There's also a prisoner who appears for the half-dozenth time to purge himself of contempt — a man who has committed no crime anyone can really name, except the crime of having been caught in this machine.
And then there's the ruined suitor from Shropshire — who periodically surfaces, Dickens says, and 'breaks out into efforts to address the Chancellor.'
'Efforts to address' — that's perfect.
Not petitions, not pleas, not arguments — efforts.
As though the simple act of communicating with the court has become a physical struggle for this man, something he has to brace himself for.
And the lawyers' clerks stand around waiting for him to furnish some fun — because that's all he is to them now.
The scene is devastating, I grant you — but I think one should be careful about what conclusions to draw from it.
Dickens is not, I would suggest, mounting a structural argument about the legal system in that passage.
He is doing what he does supremely well — rendering the human cost of institutional failure in terms of specific, unforgettable individuals.
The question of whether the Court of Chancery needs reform is rather less interesting to Dickens, I suspect, than the question of what it does to the souls of those it touches.
Which brings me to a passage I think is rather more frightening — the novel's portrait of Sir Leicester Dedlock contemplating the suit with perfect equanimity.
Sir Leicester has no objection to an interminable Chancery suit.
It is a slow, expensive, British, constitutional kind of thing.
That rhythm — slow, expensive, British, constitutional — is a list, but each item quietly cancels out the indignation of the previous one.
For Sir Leicester, 'British' and 'constitutional' are not descriptions — they are absolutions.
Edmund is exactly right about the rhythm — and it reflects something historically precise about how the governing class defended Chancery.

Every reform proposal in the first half of the nineteenth century was met with arguments almost identical to Sir Leicester's — that these institutions embodied accumulated wisdom, that to tamper with them was to invite chaos.
Dickens goes further and gives us the passage where Sir Leicester's vanity is revealed as the real foundation of his constitutional piety.
He has a shadowy impression that for his name — the name of Dedlock — to be in a cause, and not in the title of that cause, is a most ridiculous accident.
The name. The title. That's what Chancery is for, in Sir Leicester's world — it is an arena for the display of names that matter.
The ruined woman in the squeezed bonnet doesn't have a name that matters.
The Shropshire suitor doesn't have a name that matters.
Dickens understood that this wasn't incidental to the system's dysfunction — it was the system's purpose.
And there's the Wat Tyler line, which I confess I love unreasonably.
Sir Leicester concludes that to sanction any complaints about Chancery would be to encourage some person in the lower classes to rise up somewhere — like Wat Tyler.
The 'somewhere' is my favourite word in that sentence — he doesn't even know where the revolution might break out.
It's a vague, baronial dread — the peasants, massing, somewhere in the provinces.
But Dickens isn't laughing at Sir Leicester as a fool — that's the crucial thing.
He's laughing at him as a man who is precisely representative of a certain cast of mind — and it's a cast of mind that has real power over real people's lives.
I wouldn't entirely dispute that — though I'd want to resist the idea that Sir Leicester is simply a villain of the piece.
Dickens gives him a genuine dignity later — his response to Lady Dedlock's disgrace is, in its way, one of the most honourable moments in the novel.
But the passage you've both been circling speaks to something that interests me more than the political argument — it speaks to a particular kind of moral blindness.
He regards the Court of Chancery as a something devised in conjunction with a variety of other somethings by the perfection of human wisdom for the eternal settlement of everything.
'A something — in conjunction with a variety of other somethings.' The vagueness is not comic decoration — it is the diagnosis.
Sir Leicester has never had to think clearly about institutions, because for men of his class clarity was never required.

That idea of vagueness as diagnosis is a good point to carry forward — because in a moment we'll come to the passages where the system's effects become very specific indeed, through the figure of Richard Carstone.
But first — James, I want to ask about the passage in Chapter Thirty-Nine, where Dickens places Richard in Lincoln's Inn and looks back over all the men the court has already consumed.
It's one of the novel's most formally remarkable passages — and it works in a way that is almost impossible to describe without simply reading it.
Richard has just emerged from Symond's Inn into a rare patch of sunlight in Chancery Lane — Dickens notes the sunshine almost sardonically — and turns into Lincoln's Inn.
And then the narrator steps back and delivers this:

On many such loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and consumed, the life turned sour.
What strikes me is the legal precision underneath that lyrical surface.
'Chancery, which knows no wisdom but in precedent, is very rich in such precedents' — it's framed as a legal argument, almost.
The court that runs on precedent has established a precedent for ruination — and Richard is simply the next case in the series.
That list — bent head, bitten nail, lowering eye, lingering step — when you read it aloud, it accumulates like a sentence being handed down.
Each item is physical — Dickens is showing you the body before the mind goes.
And then — 'the good consuming and consumed' — which is both a description and a kind of epitaph.
You feel the active and passive simultaneously — the man is consuming himself, and being consumed by something larger.
And then Richard steps back into sunlight — 'not shabby yet, but that may come' — and Dickens leaves it there.
That parenthetical 'but that may come' is one of the most quietly devastating lines he ever wrote.
Oliver has put his finger on something important about those participles — consuming, consumed.
The moral tragedy of Richard is not that the system is wicked — though perhaps it is — but that Richard allows himself to be hollowed out by it.
There are other characters in the novel who are touched by Chancery and survive — Jarndyce himself, most notably.
The difference is character — specifically, the capacity to maintain moral purpose in the face of futility.
Richard cannot do this — and I think Dickens intends us to feel that as a moral failure, not merely a social one.
I'd push back gently on that framing — because I think it risks placing the burden of survival on the individual rather than on the institution that's destroying him.
Dickens asks directly: 'why should one be different from ten thousand?' — and that is not the question of a novelist who believes character alone determines fate.
The ten thousand are not all weaklings — they are ordinary people placed in extraordinary, engineered helplessness.
Jarndyce survives because he has money enough to insulate himself — and Dickens doesn't let us forget that.
That disagreement — between character and circumstance, between individual agency and systemic force — runs through the entire novel, and I suspect we'll be returning to it.

We've heard the formal preamble to Jarndyce and Jarndyce read aloud in the novel — 'In Chancery. Between John Jarndyce' — and there's something in the very flatness of that phrase that seems to summarise everything we've been discussing.
The machinery has a name for everyone, a slot for everyone — and that is precisely its horror.
After the break, we'll turn to the novel's other great subject — the fog itself, and what Dickens makes of atmosphere as a way of thinking about the world.

segments.title: Unravelling: How Dickens Binds It Together

utterances.text: We come now to the close of our exploration — and fittingly, we end where Bleak House itself keeps returning: to the question of how everything holds together.
A novel of this scale — nine hundred pages, dozens of characters, two narrators — should by rights collapse under its own weight.
And yet it doesn't.
Sir Edmund, I want to start with you — with the human architecture of it, the bonds of obligation and feeling that Dickens uses as connective tissue.
There's a moment in Chapter Twenty-Four where Jarndyce does something almost impossibly selfless — and it tells us everything about how Dickens imagines goodness as a structural force in the novel.
Yes, and I think this is the passage that separates the serious readers of Bleak House from those who treat it merely as a piece of social documentation.
Jarndyce calls Ada and Richard to him, and he says something which, delivered on the page, looks almost cold.
"I ask you wholly to relinquish, for the present, any tie but your relationship."
He is telling two young people who love each other to step away from that love — for their own protection.
And the force of that act is precisely that it costs him nothing materially and everything emotionally.
Dickens understands — as Burke understood — that the moral bonds between persons are the only architecture that outlasts institutions.
Chancery will grind on. Jarndyce's goodness is the only thing in this novel that does not corrode.
I'd agree with that, though I'd frame it slightly differently.
What Dickens is showing us in that scene is the vacuum created by institutional failure.
Jarndyce steps in as a kind of private court of equity because the actual Court of Equity — Chancery — is simply no longer functioning as a court of conscience.
That's historically precise: the real Chancery of Dickens' era had become procedurally self-serving — a machine for generating fees rather than resolving disputes.
And then later — in Chapter Fifty-Four, which is as close to a courtroom scene as the novel gives us — we see Sir Leicester, stripped of everything except his dignity, looking to Bucket.
Dickens writes — and this is a quietly devastating line —
"Sir Leicester Dedlock remains immovable, with the same icy surface upon him, except that he once or twice looks towards Mr. Bucket, as relying on that officer alone of all mankind."
An aristocrat with ancient lineage, a baronetcy, the full apparatus of class — reduced to one hired detective as his sole point of human trust.
That is the novel's binding mechanism laid bare: all the formal structures have failed, and what remains is personal loyalty — which is, of course, also purchased.
Purchased, yes — but Dickens allows Bucket something more than mercenary competence, I think.
There's a genuine respect in that gaze of Sir Leicester's — even admiration — for a man of no class who possesses every virtue Leicester's class is supposed to embody.
Dickens is not quite the leveller he is sometimes painted.
He believes in character — individual, inalienable character — wherever in the social hierarchy it happens to manifest.
And of course, threading through all of this — above every character who trusts or fails to trust — is Tulkinghorn.
The man who binds it all together by never binding himself to anyone.
Dickens introduces him at sunset — which is already doing a great deal of atmospheric work — approaching Sir Leicester and Lady Dedlock at the usual methodical pace.
And then comes this extraordinary passage, which I have read aloud probably two hundred times and it still gives me a slight chill:
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
"He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
His own client.
That's a legal joke and a philosophical abyss in three words.
It's also legally precise in a rather unsettling way.
A solicitor's fiduciary duty runs to his client — and only to his client.
By making himself his own client, Tulkinghorn has constructed a situation of perfect, hermetic self-interest — and it's entirely within the professional logic of his world.
Dickens isn't satirising Tulkinghorn as a deviation from the legal profession. He's suggesting Tulkinghorn is its ideal expression.
And what I find endlessly marvellous about that passage, from a performer's standpoint, is the parenthetical.
"He wears his usual expressionless mask — if it be a mask."
Four words — and Dickens has just undermined the entire metaphor he was relying on.
Perhaps that blankness is not concealment. Perhaps it is simply what he is.
That's darker than anything a mask could suggest.
Which is why, when he dies, one feels — not grief exactly, but a kind of atmospheric disturbance.
As if a pressure that had been present throughout the novel suddenly lifts — and the air is not fresher, merely different.
And there is Lady Dedlock, too — that extraordinary passage in Chapter Two where Dickens turns the satirist's scalpel on the whole apparatus of aristocratic self-delusion.
She believes herself inscrutable — and everyone around her has mapped her completely.
That tension — between the performance of mystery and the banality of being utterly known — connects her to Tulkinghorn in a way Dickens never makes quite explicit.
Oh, that Chapter Two passage about Lady Dedlock and her dressmakers and jewellers — I could live in that passage.
Dickens is in full comic flight, but the joke has real teeth.
He builds to this image — of the tradespeople who flatter and defer and humbly affect to follow —
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
The aristocracy as a miniature fleet, towed away by their own servants.
It's devastating and delicious in equal measure — which is Dickens at his best.
And the detail of the tradespeople is historically exact: Blaze and Sparkle, Sheen and Gloss — Dickens invented the names, but not the practice.
The luxury trades of the 1840s and 1850s operated precisely on this system — of cultivated dependence, of manufactured prestige.
What Dickens sees — and this is where his genius lies — is that the fashion system and the legal system are structurally identical.
Both exist ostensibly to serve their clients. Both exist actually to perpetuate themselves.
That structural parallelism — it really does feel like Dickens's great formal achievement in this novel, doesn't it.
Everything mirrors everything else: the fog in Chancery and the fog of class, the secrets kept by solicitors and the secrets kept by the self.
Sir Edmund, a final thought from you — what holds this novel together, at its deepest level?
Character. Always character.
The systems — Chancery, fashion, the law — are the novel's subject matter. But they are not the novel's animating principle.
What Dickens trusts — what he has always trusted — is that in the midst of every corrupt institution, there will be an Esther, a Jarndyce, a Bucket.
Imperfect, various, stubbornly human — and utterly resistant to the fog.
Imperfect, various, stubbornly human — I think that may be the best possible note on which to close.
My warmest thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — for bringing such care, such knowledge, and such evident pleasure to this extraordinary novel.
Bleak House rewards every reading. We hope this one has sent you back to the page.

Wintry morning, looking with dull eyes and sallow face upon the
neighbourhood of Leicester Square, finds its inhabitants unwilling to
get out of bed. Many of them are not early risers at the brightest of
times, being birds of night who roost when the sun is high and are
wide awake and keen for prey when the stars shine out. Behind dingy
blind and curtain, in upper story and garret, skulking more or less
under false names, false hair, false titles, false jewellery, and
false histories, a colony of brigands lie in their first sleep.
Gentlemen of the green-baize road who could discourse from personal
experience of foreign galleys and home treadmills; spies of strong
governments that eternally quake with weakness and miserable fear,
broken traitors, cowards, bullies, gamesters, shufflers, swindlers,
and false witnesses; some not unmarked by the branding-iron beneath
their dirty braid; all with more cruelty in them than was in Nero,
and more crime than is in Newgate. For howsoever bad the devil can be
in fustian or smock-frock (and he can be very bad in both), he is a
more designing, callous, and intolerable devil when he sticks a pin
in his shirt-front, calls himself a gentleman, backs a card or
colour, plays a game or so of billiards, and knows a little about
bills and promissory notes, than in any other form he wears. And in
such form Mr. Bucket shall find him, when he will, still pervading
the tributary channels of Leicester Square.
